newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
SUGAR: World market for October 22, 1996

White sugar futures ended mostly easier but well off the lows in modest volume. Hurricane Lili caused little excitement with the Cubans still aiming at a higher crop in 1996/97. December closed 70 cents easier at $316.70 a tonne, while March finished 50 cents weaker at $313.60 per tonne.

In New York raw sugar futures ended modestly higher buoyed by local and speculative buying. March added 6 points to close at 10.63 cents/lb, while May finished 4 points higher at 10.65 cents/lb. The balance closed 4 to 5 points higher. There was no fundamental reason for the rise especially with Brazil freeing the remaining 1.04 million tonnes from the export tax, which could keep prices under pressure on Wednesday. FUNDAMENTALS

PAKISTAN - In spite of a five to six per cent higher area planted to cane, sugar production in 1996/97 could be lower than had been expected. While originally it had been estimated that production could be at around 2.9 million tonnes, in white value terms, compared to 2.5 million tonnes the previous year, observers have now become much more pessimistic and a crop of not more than 2.5 million tonnes is not excluded.

The original estimate was based on the increase in sugar cane area but a drought and a very heavy attack of top and stem borers has occurred in many parts of the country which will adversely affect cane yield and sugar content.

Moreover, there is a strong demand for gur, which is most likely exported to Afghanistan and Central Asian states. Prices for gur are very attractive and hence large scale diversion of cane to gur manufacturers must be expected, which will reduce the raw material basis for the mill sector. However, close observers of the industry warn that a clearer picture will not emerge before the middle of December.

CHINA - According to preliminary figures, China imported 13,283 tonnes of sugar, raw value, in September 1996, the first month of the 1996/97 crop year, which compares to 361,000 tonnes imported the same month the previous year. Total imports in crop year 1995/96 (September/August) reached 1.9 million tonnes, down from 2.9 million tonnes the previous year.

Sugar exports in September 1996 reached 103,368 tonnes, up from 32,400 tonnes exported the same month the previous year. Total exports in crop year 1995/96 reached 830,200 tonnes, up from 540,000 tonnes exported in 1994/95 but down on the 1.1 million tonnes exported in 1993/94.

BRAZIL - The Brazilian government set exports at 5.2 million tonnes of sugar, tel quel, in its 1996/97 crop plan, but only exempted initial 4.2 million tonnes from tax. Liberating the remaining 1.0 million tonnes was left to a later date to give the authorities an opportunity to monitor the harvest and in particular the supply of alcohol.

Given favourable production prospects, the government now authorized the additional 1.04 million tonnes to be sold exempt of export tax. Of the total, 735,600 tonnes can be exported from the centre/south region and 304,400 tonnes from the north/northeast region. Centre/south producers, where the harvest began in mid-April, have recently been pushing the government to release exemptions for the remaining quota so that they can make fresh sales.

CUBA - Cuban sugar minister Nelson Torres said that the country still aimed to increase sugar production in the upcoming 1996/97 harvest despite large areas of cane flattened or flooded by hurricane Lili. Until the hurricane, Cuban authorities had hoped for a crop of 5.2 to 5.3 million tonnes, up from the 4.5 million tonnes produced the previous year.

Torres said that once flooded cane fields had been drained, some cane would stand again. The cane that remained on the ground would just have to be cut as it was, he said, adding that a good part of the affected cane would be recoverable. Hurricane Lili also caused partial damage, mainly to roofs, at 56 of the country's 156 sugar mills. But Torres said it was too early to predict this would end up affecting production.

EUROPE - Rains increased across much of Europe during the week ended October 22. Most of the rain amounts were only 6 to 25 mm, but 75 to 155 mm inundated northern Italy. The harvest continued to make progress despite the light showers in some areas. Yield potential in most areas has been enhanced slightly due to recent warm and dry conditions and favourable harvesting weather.

In the former Soviet Union, sugar beet areas had only very light showers during the week ended October 22. The region has seen rain receipts of only 25 to 50 per cent, thus far this month. This allowed harvesting to finally begin making some good progress. No frost damage has been reported so far.

GERMANY - The amount of beets processed into sugar in the week ended October 18, was again below the previous year, but due to a considerably higher sugar content overall sugar production was up. Cumulative 1996 beet deliveries amounted to 7.93 million tonnes against 7.36 million tonnes in 1995 and 7.53 million tonnes in 1994.
The estimate for total deliveries for 1996/97 stands unchanged at 26.433 million tonnes, up on last year's actual total of 26.049 million tonnes and the 1994/95 result of 24.211 million tonnes.

Sugar content (17.88 per cent) is sharply up on last year's 16.54 per cent and also significantly above the 1994 result of 16.61 per cent. Sugar production so far amounted to 1.286 million tonnes, raw value, against 1.084 million tonnes in 1995 and 1.119 million tonnes in 1994.

POLAND - The latest Polish beet test results of October 7, show that the dry and sunny weather in September boosted sugar content while root weight is slightly down on the previous year. Sugar content amounted to 16.54 per cent, up from last year's 15.98 per cent and the 1994 result of 14.24 per cent.
Root weight reached 883 grams against 900 grams in 1995 and 723 grams in 1994. This resulted in a theoretical sugar weight per root of 146 grams against 144 grams in 1995 and 103 grams in 1994.
Due to a largely increased area sown to beet and the good shape of the beets, the country is heading for a very good crop.
